read.bigIdea: A style is a description, not a recipe.
read.where: The Beer Judge Certification Program’s **2021 guidelines** run from **1. Standard American Beer** to **34. Specialty Beer**. Categories group styles with **similar judging characteristics**, not a shared history, so a category can hold beers from different countries. Each style gives an **Overall Impression**, then **Aroma, Appearance, Flavor, Mouthfeel**, comments, history, characteristic ingredients, a **style comparison**, vital statistics and **commercial examples**. They’re written mainly for **homebrew competitions**, and commercial beers don’t have to fit them, so use the guidelines to **describe** and **compare**, not to police labels.
read.mixup: A BJCP category isn’t a family tree. Styles share a category because they’re judged alike.

video.title: Beer Statistics Explained - ABV, ABW, IBU, SRM

read.where: Every BJCP style lists **vital statistics**: **Original Gravity** (how dense with sugar the wort was before fermenting), **Final Gravity** (after), **ABV**, **IBU** (International Bittering Units) and color in **SRM** (Standard Reference Method). The BJCP calls them **guidelines, not absolutes**: they help judges order a flight, not disqualify a beer. Example, **American IPA** (21A): OG **1.056–1.070**, FG **1.008–1.014**, IBU **40–70**, SRM **6–14**, ABV **5.5–7.5%**. Compare **Märzen**: IBU **18–24**, ABV **5.6–6.3%**: the numbers show the malt-forward beer before you taste it.
read.mixup: IBU isn’t the whole story. Malt sweetness balances bitterness, so two beers with the same IBUs can taste quite different.

video.title: Intro to 2018 AHA/BJCP Scoresheets and Tips for Efficient Judging

read.bigIdea: Fifty points, mostly aroma and flavor.
read.where: BJCP judges score a beer out of **50**: **Aroma 12**, **Appearance 3**, **Flavor 20**, **Mouthfeel 5**, **Overall Impression 10**. The order matters: smell it **as soon as it’s poured** (aroma fades as it warms), look at it, smell again, then taste. The BJCP’s bands: **Excellent 38–44**, **Very Good 30–37**, **Good 21–29**, **Drinkable 14–20**, **Problem 13 or lower**; **45–50** is kept for world-class beers. Judges at a table aim to land within **7 points** of each other. Use the same sheet with the team: it trains people to describe a beer in order, not just say “good”.
read.mixup: Appearance is only 3 of 50 points. A pretty beer with a flawed aroma still scores low.

sections.name: Pairing the menu with the chef

video.title: How Chefs Can Lead In Beer & Food Pairing

keyPoints.line: delicate with delicate, big with big.

read.bigIdea: Taste the dish and the beer together.
read.where: At this level you pair the **whole menu**, with the chef. Start where Levels 1 and 2 did: match **strength** (delicate dishes with delicate beers, rich with bold), then pick the job: **complement** (shared flavors, like roast with chocolate), **contrast**, or **cut** (carbonation, bitterness and acid lift fat). Watch the traps: **bitterness** can turn metallic with oily fish. Then sit down with the chef and **taste each pair together**; adjust the beer or the garnish. For a **beer dinner**, the Brewers Association suggests **3–4 oz** per course, building intensity through the meal.
read.mixup: A pairing on paper isn’t a pairing. Taste them together: the sauce and seasoning change the match.
read.sayIt: With the short rib, try the porter: the roast picks up the char on the meat.
